parts.label: (a)
key_concepts: Fleming's left-hand rule for motor force
hints: Hint 1: Look carefully at the side view - which way does the magnetic field point between the N pole and the S pole, and which way does the conventional current point along the wire?
Hint 2: If you can find the direction of the magnetic force on the current-carrying wire, think about what the wire must do back to the magnets that produce the field.
parts.proper_answer: The force on the wire is vertically upwards, so by Newton's third law the force on the magnets is vertically downwards.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Find the field and current directions**
In the side view the N pole is on one side and the S pole on the other, so the magnetic field $B$ between them points from N to S, into the plane of the side view. The conventional current $I$ points to the right.

Step 2: **Get the force on the wire**
Put Fleming's left hand with First finger along $B$ (into the page) and second finger along $I$ (to the right). Your thumb then points upwards. So the magnetic force on the wire is upwards.

Step 3: **Use Newton to get the force on the magnets**
The magnet exerts an upward force on the wire. By Newton's third law the wire exerts an equal and opposite force on the magnet system. $$F_{magnet} = -F_{wire}$$ So the force on the magnets is vertically downwards.

parts.label: (b)(i)
key_concepts: magnetic force F = BIL sin theta
length of conductor in uniform field
hints: Hint 1: Focus only on the short section of wire that is actually inside the uniform field - what is its length in metres and what is the angle between current and field when $\theta = 90^{\circ}$?
Hint 2: Check all your SI conversions before multiplying - $B$ is given in mT and the pole width is given in cm.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Recall the maximum force condition**
When the wire is perpendicular to the field, $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ and $\sin \theta = 1$. The force is maximum: $$F = BIL$$

Step 2: **Insert values in SI units**
$B = 3.7 \text{ mT} = 3.7 \times 10^{-3} \text{ T}$, $I = 5.1 \text{ A}$, $L = 8.5 \text{ cm} = 8.5 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$. $$F = (3.7 \times 10^{-3}) \times 5.1 \times (8.5 \times 10^{-2})$$ $$F = 1.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N}$$ This is the magnitude of the force on the wire.

parts.label: (b)(ii)
hints: Hint 1: The wire is now slanted so more wire sits in the field, but only the component of length perpendicular to the field counts - see how $L = 8.5/\sin 60^{\circ}$ combines with $\sin 60^{\circ}$ in $F = BIL\sin\theta$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **See why the angle cancels out**
For an angle $\theta$ the general rule is: $$F = BI L \sin \theta$$ Here the length in the field is larger: $$L = \frac{8.5 \times 10^{-2}}{\sin 60^{\circ}}$$ So: $$F = BI \times \frac{8.5 \times 10^{-2}}{\sin 60^{\circ}} \times \sin 60^{\circ} = BI \times 8.5 \times 10^{-2}$$ The $\sin 60^{\circ}$ terms cancel, leaving exactly the same calculation as in (b)(i), $1.6 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N}$.

parts.label: (c)
key_concepts: alternating current and peak vs r.m.s.
hints: Hint 1: Since $F = BIL$ at $90^{\circ}$, the force at any instant is directly proportional to the instantaneous current - so what shape must the $F$-$t$ graph have if $I$-$t$ is sinusoidal?
Hint 2: Work out the time for one full cycle from the 20 Hz frequency, then double it for the two cycles you need to show.
Hint 3: Remember the given 5.1 A is now an r.m.s. value, not the peak - how do you get the peak current and hence the peak force for your graph scale?
parts.proper_answer: Sinusoidal $F$-$t$ graph starting at 0, with two full cycles, period $T = 0.050 \text{ s}$, peak force $F_0 = \sqrt{2} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-3} = 2.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Link force to alternating current**
With $\theta = 90^{\circ}$, $F = BIL$ at every instant, so $F$ follows $I$ exactly. An alternating current $I = I_0 \sin \omega t$ gives an alternating force: $$F = BI_0L \sin \omega t = F_0 \sin \omega t$$ So the graph is a sine wave through zero, going positive and negative as the current reverses.

Step 2: **Find the period**
Frequency $f = 20 \text{ Hz}$, so: $$T = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{20} = 0.050 \text{ s}$$ Two cycles therefore last $0.10 \text{ s}$. Draw two complete sine waves in that time.

Step 3: **Find the amplitude from r.m.s. current**
For a sine wave, peak = $\sqrt{2} \times$ r.m.s. $$I_0 = \sqrt{2} \times 5.1 = 7.21 \text{ A}$$ Force amplitude scales the same way: $$F_0 = \sqrt{2} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-3} = 2.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N}$$ Label the $F$-axis with $+2.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N}$ and $-2.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ N}$ peaks and the $t$-axis with $0.05 \text{ s}$, $0.10 \text{ s}$.
